Mr. Speaker, under S.O. 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to discuss an urgent matter.
Considering that the CBC refuses to broadcast advertisements designed to inform the consumer, and I am referring to the French advertisement sponsored by credit unions and the Consumer Protection Board under the slogan "Le gros bon sens"; considering also that the privately owned TV network saw fit to air those advertisements which are partly free, thus recognizing the importance of informing the consumer; and finally, considering that the state network gets subsidies from public funds and that its audience is entitled to the same services, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle):
That the House unanimously urge the Secretary of State to suggest that the CBC change its code of ethics to allow the broadcasting of advertisements which consumers are entitled to.

The point is that there has been an effort in both pieces of legislation dealing with grain and other crops to treat producers in exactly the same way, especially in relation to interest. If the advance is repaid in the normal fashion as contemplated by the legislation and as has been demonstrated by our experience with the grain legislation, then of course interest is not payable. But in a case where the advance is in default, or where the producer chooses to repay it in terms of cash instead of the delivery of crop, then of course the advance does begin to attract interest.
It is probably important once again that members know the history of that particular provision which really results from the experience with the grain legislation. Originally the cash advance legislation dealing with grain did not contain a provision calling for the payment of interest. It was upon the recommendation of farmers and farm organizations that that provision was put in, in order to avoid what otherwise would be an abuse of legislation if an advance were taken with no intention of delivering the grain but rather in order to have the advance as an interest-free loan to be used for other purposes.
Farmers and farm organizations in western Canada perceived that as an abuse of the legislation, and recommended that the cash advance legislation relating to grain should be changed to recognize that problem. The amendments were made to the legislation a considerable time ago. Obviously they have been very well received and very widely approved. The legislation the Minister of Agriculture is now presenting is of course legislation which follows upon exactly the same principle. It does not specifically relate to grain, but of course expands the principle so that it will relate to a number of other crops across Canada whether they be produced in western Canada or in any other part of the country.
I think the principle the Minister of Agriculture has put before the House in the form of this particular legislation is very good; it is sound. This is a principle which I think farmers in parts of Canada who are not used to the grains industry on the prairies will welcome when they see this kind of provision, and I know producers across the country are very anxious to see this legislation proceed through the House of Commons and the Standing Committee on Agriculture so that the advantages of cash advances for crops, other than grains, will become available to farmers across the country.

It is significant too that in that period, beginning in the early seventies, the Canadian Wheat Board was encouraged by (She government and the minister responsible to pursue vigorously as we in Canada had never done before international markets for barley and feed grains. We are now a significant exporter of those particular grains and it is because of those efforts in the early seventies to win, keep and service those markets that we now have these very important markets for western Canadian feed grain producers.
We have as well the annual commitment by the government of Canada of $10 million toward a new market development fund to enhance grain marketing opportunities at home and abroad. Farmers and their organizations, as well as others, have taken advantage of this fund to develop and find new marketing opportunities.
We have as well new research facilities. I know my hon. friends opposite are very interested in this subject and we have joined in discussions on this question in the Standing Committee on Agriculture previously. Obviously research is an important matter in the field of agriculture and in this area we have seen some important developments, such as the new crop science division at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon which is doing significant work in the field of agricultural research, in addition to the normal research facilities of the Canadian Department of Agriculture. I think as well of the new protein-oil-starch pilot plant in Saskatoon which will shortly be doing important new work in developing new ways of processing our grains and oil seeds.
Then there is the two-price wheat program which was the subject of debate in previous sessions of this parliament. This was an important measure which, long after the hubbub of debate in the House subsided, has established very clearly its relevance and has paid dividends to western Canadian agriculture.
In the same period that we have been working on these matters, we have also substantially increased ttyg level of available cash advances to the western grain industry and have improved the ways in which those advances can be repaid. This, of course, refers to the amendments discussed in this House and approved by the House of Commons in previous sessions of parliament, under which legislation the available level of cash advances was increased to $15,000, with the repayment terms for farmers being made more broad and flexible, so that if farmers wished to avail themselves of the legislation cash advances could be more tailored to their

particular needs and to the way they ran their farming operations. That is probably a small, technical change which has taken place during the last few years, but an important one, one that shows the general upgrading and improvement of facilities available to western agriculture.
Of additional interest are the improvements in the timing of Canadian Wheat Board final payments and adjustment cheques. Often times in the past it seemed that these cheques would come at an unfortunate time, or at least not at the right time so far as the planning of a farmer's income and tax position was concerned. Amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act have corrected that particular situation and prevented the rather unfortunate development which occurred a couple of years ago when some farmers were perhaps caught by surprise and received two final payments in the one taxation year. In some cases this served to defeat their tax planning. It is, of course, the intention to make that income position as certain as it possibly can be, and changes in the Wheat Board Act have been passed by this parliament to deal with that particular aspect. I think as well of the implementation of the deferred cash ticket option for grain producers on the delivery of their grain so that, again, they can exercise greater control over their income position.
In another area I would mention the development which began to take place four years ago with the provision of reliable production and marketing information for producers to be placed in their hands in the spring, well in advance of seeding time. It is important that a farmer should be able to take advantage of that information to plan his production and marketing for the coming year. Because of a practice which has been implemented by the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, with the co-operation of the Department of Agriculture and the Wheat Board, information is compiled, prepared, and distributed to each farmer in the prairie region early in March each year so that he can have the best information which is available to production and marketing experts, and farmers can them make their own decisions based on the material they have.
Determined efforts have been made to remove the longstanding inequities which have existed in our system of domestic feed grains marketing in the past. This has been the subject of extensive and sometimes heated debate in the House, and it is important to remember that the government has now for many months been endeavouring to find that important national consensus as to the proper shape of a domestic feed grains marketing policy which will, with equity and effectiveness, meet the needs of grain producers and others engaged in agriculture in both the west and the east.
I think of another achievement which is significant in the establishment of a separate marketing pool for malting barley effective for the crop year 1975-76. This again has been the subject of discussion in the House of Commons earlier in the session.

I think we should also consider the very important point that the legislation before us this afternoon is legislation that applies to farmers generally all across Canada, the expansion of something that has been available in western Canada with respect to grains for some considerable length of time, and has been very well received and approved by the farmers of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I feel obliged to speak briefly on Bill C-2 which provides for advance payments with respect to crops other than those administered by the Canadian Wheat Board in its designated area. As my colleague said, it is nice to see the two ministers opposite who share responsibility for the agricultural industry sitting next to one another, conferring and doing their best to pilot this bill through the House. That, of course, immediately brings to mind something we have often discussed in the agricultural committee, the division of responsibility in certain fields of agriculture between the minister responsible for the Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). We all know of the difficulties connected with the administration of agricultural policy. However, the division of responsibility leads to duplication and overlapping, evident especially in legislation and programs relating to all agriculture in Canada.
I remind the minister that he was not able to listen to part of my speech in the throne speech debate. 1 had hoped, when he introduced the legislation, that he would refute the implication in the Speech from the Throne that this is the only legislation we shall see during the present session of parliament relating to agriculture. He did not deal with that matter when he spoke in the throne speech debate.
As I said previously, the Speech from the Throne is little but a philosophical exposition of what the government intends to place before parliament for dealing with various aspects of the economy and other matters. The particular bill we are now debating is, I submit, the only agricultural bill to which the Speech from the Throne makes reference. Where it would be of advantage is on those commodities that can be stored beyond the normal sales period. Many of them can be held for considerably less than 12 months. The cash advance was paid so as to provide the farmer with enough money to produce the second crop. In all cases we wrote in protection which allowed the Wheat Board to collect the advance when the sales were made, and if the sales were not made in the second year, then the cash advance could be paid out again on the second crop. Why cannot these regulations be spelled out in the legislation itself rather than being left to the Minister of Agriculture and the governor in council?
There will be a great requirement for adequate administration if this program is to work. I am reminded of a story I read long ago. I believe it was in "Uncle Tom's Cabin", one of the slaves had to weigh his cotton at the end of the day's work and, if his cotton did not weigh up, he did not receive his rations. I fear that this is what the Minister of Agriculture will do by regulation, that is, he will demand that there be producer marketing boards or producer groups in control of the producer if the producer is to qualify for any payment.
Reference was made to the Canadian Wheat Board and to the distribution of advance payments through that medium. The key to the success of that program is the permit book. I would warn all producers who become involved in this program to ensure they do not lose any of the freedom which they are justly proud of at the present time. They will have to exercise a
Advance Payments for Crops
great deal of good judgment when they enter this program because, as good as the program may be, all commodities do not fall into the same category as grain. I think, for instance, of the man in Prince Edward Island who two years ago had to destroy his whole crop because he could not find a market for it.
What happens to the producer if he has taken the advance payment and does not find a market for his produce? This is the reason I say there must be regulations spelled out to deal with situations and circumstances which are bound to arise because there is such a differential between the movement and sale of grain and the movement and sale of other perishable farm products.
The hon. member for Elgin referred to the situation when the repayment is made in the form of cash rather than through the sale of produce. From my reading of the bill, if a producer decides to make the repayment in cash rather than in produce he would not have to pay interest on the first $500 or 10 per cent of the advance payment. I ask why the producer of perishable and other farm produce should be treated differently than the grain producer? In last year's Bill C-10, which was brought in by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, it is particularly spelled out that the producer and each such shareholder, partner or member, jointly and severally guarantee repayment of the full amount in default, together with interest thereon at the appropriate prescribed rate per annum from the date of the making of the advance payment, in the event of a default by the actual producer. There would seem to be an inconsistency here. I do not know the reason for it.
Perhaps the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Minister of Agriculture are still not communicating in an effort to bring in policies that are consistent. For the life of me I cannot understand why there should be a differential here. Therefore I believe there will have to be a fair amount of dialogue in respect to this bill prior to its passage.
The government really is not guaranteeing that there will be an adequate price for the product when it is sold. It would be far better if the producer did not have to rely on advance payments. Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few brief remarks on the bill before the House today. The first thing I want to do is to agree with the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) that the bill as drafted is rather complicated and fails to answer a lot of questions. Once we get to the committee stage we may be able to get some of the answers from the minister and make final judgment.
The other thing that I wanted to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member for Elgin has already talked about it, is that the minister should consult more closely with the farm organizations. It seems to me this is a very important part of governing people-seeking consensus from various organizations relative to one's portfolio. It seems to me the knowledge farm organizations have of this bill at the moment is not very great.
As far as the bill itself is concerned, we support the principle, the intent of the bill to make cash advances available to more farmers for more products. It is something that we in this party have talked about for many years as likely to be of some help to a number of farmers in Canada who are not eligible under the present cash advance program which is restricted to the Wheat Board area in western Canada. There are a couple of things, though, that I do have some concern about after looking at the bill very quickly.
I notice there is a ceiling limiting to $15,000 cash advances to any one person or operator. I understand the maximum number of people working in a unit can be three, which means that in some cases larger co-operative farms would be excluded from this legislation because, as I understand it, they only qualify for a cash advance when not more than three people are participating in the operation of a co-operative farm. Now there might be six or seven families participating in the running of a farm and it seems to me this is one of the areas we should examine in committee to see whether or not we might amend that clause in the bill.
The other question that occurs to me is whether or not the cash advances pertain to corporations, to companies such as Heinz, which might be involved in a certain aspect of farming. Would they qualify for an interest-free cash advance when they really do not need one? Or is the scheme limited to the ordinary producer, the ordinary family farmer? These are
(Mr. Wise.]
some of the things that cross my mind as I take a quick look at the bill.
The other point I wanted to make is that a bill such as the one before us today, albeit it is going in the right direction, is by no means the answer to the problems farmers face. Many people say: "Well, things are very good; out in the prairies the price of grain is very high; farmers are doing well; they do not have many problems." But farm income historically goes up and down like a yo-yo. It is about time the government brought in more adequate farm income stabilization programs covering not just prairie grains or certain crops in Ontario but all farm products in this country so that farmers would enjoy support and stability of income. In this way more people would be staying on the land and there would be greater production of food in this country. All we need to do is look at the statistics concerning farmers leaving the land.
Farmers are still leaving the land at a very alarming rate and we are not going to keep them on the land just through an expansion of the cash advance program. What we need is a farm income stability program. We could use the model in British Columbia as one very good example brought in by the provincial NDP government. That is something that could be copied here in Ottawa at the federal level.
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) really wants to keep farmers on the land he has to resolve some of the other problems such as the problem presently afflicting cow-calf operators. The federal government should be paying a lot more attention to this problem and coming forth with a program costing tens of millions of dollars to support cow-calf operators, to fill some of the gaps in some of the provincial programs that are already in existence. That is one way of helping the ordinary farmer in this country.
Another point, and 1 know the minster shares my views on this, is that we should be looking at the feasibility of a national marketing agency forecast to help the cow-calf operator, to give him some security and some collective process in the market place. These are things we have to look at in the long term if we really want to help the food producer in Canada. Cash advances are only a very small part of helping producers. If we want to help the farmers, we have to keep them on the land, and we will keep them on the land by guaranteeing them an income. If we fail to do this farms are going to be larger and larger and agro-business will become more and more powerful. In the long run this will hurt not only the small rural community but it will hurt the consumer in the price he pays for food at the receiving end.
Rather than go on at length at this time I should like to hear some more spokespeople from the Liberal side, perhaps the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, answering some of the questions that have been raised, before participating at the committee level in terms of asking precise questions about the way in which this bill would apply to the various produce groups across Canada.

On this point my department will take appropriate measures to guarantee that such organizations do, in fact, represent a significant portion of the crop in that area. It must also satisfy the government that it will repay the money borrowed to make advance payments. The act covers all the possibilities of producer default, but the experience of the Prairie Grain Advance Program indicated that there is a very small percentage of producers who ever default on the advance payments.
In the case of producers the portion of the crop on which an advance payment is made is to be stored by the producer, either on his own premises, on another farm or commercially, providing the grain is stored in his own name. A producer cannot receive an advance if he is in arrears or in default for a previous advance.
Applications for advance payments must be made before a set date and must include all relevant information as required by the act. The maximum amount advanced in any crop year to one producer eligible under the act is $15,000. Multifarmer units can receive a maximum of $30,000 or $45,000, depending on the number of parties involved. These levels have been established similarly to those under Prairie Grain Advance Payments.
Yet in all cases the amount of an advance payment possible under this act cannot exceed one half of the unit market price payable for that crop in that crop year. For example, if Ontario wheat is selling at $3.50 a bushel, and I use this only to show what we will be lending, then the payment can be up to $1.75 a bushel in the first year.
The logic behind Bill C-2 is not new for Canadian agriculture. The act would ease the cash flow to farmers of storable crops when they need it most. However, there are many other similar programs in agriculture which provide stability to farmers.
In addition to the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act, mentioned previously, we also have the Western Grain Stabilization Act which helps to protect western grain farmers from large, unexpected declines in returns from the production and sale of their grain. Such drops in the market are caused by factors beyond the control of both the farmer and the government.
Furthermore, the Farm Credit Corporation makes available large amounts of money to producers to assist them in establishing and developing sound farm enterprises. The Agricultural Stabilization Act provides a miminum support level for named commodities under the act at 90 per cent of the previous five-year average. In addition, other commodities can be designated for support if the need arises.
We also have a Crop Insurance Act which provides Canadian producers with insurance in the case of crop damage or failure. Most farmers use this program every year. The
[Mr. Whelan.)
Agricultural Product Co-operative Marketing Act is designed to encourage and protect co-operative marketing of Canadian agricultural commodities.
All these measures are meant to help farmers cope with the many risks and uncertainties of agricultural production. However, consumers as well benefit from these various programs because the market will be supplied in a much more orderly fashion.
In Bill C-2, by providing Canadian producers of storable crops with a way to ease their cash flow problems, the government is stabilizing crop production levels. This in turn will ensure year-round availability of Canadian food products at reasonable costs to Canadian consumers.
Instead of having to depend on imported food products, we will assist Canadian producers by providing controlled atmospheric temperature storage where it will be possible to store fresh vegetables as long as eight months. This will enable us to supply many of the commodities it is now necessary to import.
A good example of this is cabbage. According to research conducted in my department over a period of years, cabbage that has been stored for several months is in as good a condition or better when removed from storage. This is also true of potatoes, several million dollars worth of which have been stored in.the last two years. The province of British Columbia has used the largest share of money available for this; however, other provinces are now participating in this program.
Up to this time it has been necessary to borrow the money required to finance this operation until the commodities have been sold. When this bill becomes law, producers of storable crops will have the same type of program that has been available to western farmers under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. This is a step forward, something I have been promising for some time. It will be beneficial to many farmers in all parts of Canada, as well as Canadian consumers who will be able to purchase these Canadian products. Therefore I strongly urge my colleagues in the House to support Bill C-2, and I trust that it will receive approval and speedy passage in the House.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I have promised for some time to bring in a program that would help relieve financial pressure on producers of storable crops in Canada. Bill C-2 was written with that purpose in mind.
Advance Payments for Crops
Since 1958 producers of wheat, oats and barley in the Canadian Wheat Board designated area have been able to receive advance payments under the provisions of the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. The program has worked very well and western grain farmers have benefited greatly. The act has improved the cash flow to grain farmers particularly after the critical harvest period and when low Canadian Wheat Board quotas restricted deliveries. Western grain farmers face delivery restrictions after harvest, but they have the benefit of the PGAP program under which they can receive interest-free advance payments on undelivered grain.
Wheat, oats and barley sold to the Canadian Wheat Board in its designated area are the only three crops in Canada for which this privilege is extended. Yet all other grain producers and producers of storable crops face the same market glut and storage problems that hit western grain farmers during the post-harvest period. Most storable crops produced in Canada are not subject to the marketing quota controls and price pooling schemes available for wheat, oats and barley. As a result, markets for these crops are often depressed, particularly during the months immediately following harvest.
Producers have incurred most of their total production costs by harvest time and they must then find money to pay off their debts. Often they will rush to sell just enough of their crop to cover their production costs. Accordingly, market congestion or depressed prices result, and a lot of people count on it. This can needlessly depress returns to farmers during this period. In addition it can result in loss of efficiency in marketing and loss of profitability. This is why producers of storable crops, including producers of wheat, oats and barley in regions other than the Canadian Wheat Board designated area have requested a similar opportunity of receiving interest-free advances.
The objective of the Advance Payments for Crops Act, known as Bill C-2, is designed to extend the existing program for wheat, oats and barley in the Canadian Wheat Board designated area, to all other storable crops such as Ontario wheat, white beans, tree fruits, cole and root crops, tobacco, soybeans, horticultural crops, et cetera, in the rest of Canada including those in the wheat board designated area.
The act will provide the legislative authority for the federal government to guarantee the repayment of advance payments on storable crops. In addition it will guarantee the interest on such advance payments when they are made in accordance with the provisions of the act.
The government proposes in Bill C-2 that, where a producer organization intends to make an advance payment to a producer out of money borrowed from a bank for that purpose, the government will guarantee repayment of the advances, including the interest being charged. In case of producer defaults, we would not be liable for more than one half the price of applicable crops.

Again I have to confess to mixed emotions in bidding farewell to a friend and colleague who has been in this House for almost 15 years. During that time we have fought together in many political wars. I can only admire his grit and tenacity in marching off to yet another battle.
The hon. member has forged for himself a special place in this Chamber, and, indeed, in the minds of individual Canadians across this country. He is a politician of tremendous heart and eloquence, as befits his Irish ancestry. My first point is this: while Standing Order 15(2) states that the House shall proceed to the "ordinary daily routine of proceedings" at 3 p.m., or noon as the case may be, it states with equal force that "not later than 2.15 p.m., or 11.15 a.m., as the case may be, oral questions shall be taken up." The time 3 p.m. was inserted for the protection of the government, and 2.15 p.m. for the protection of the opposition parties, under the operation of the rule. It is surely anomalous that the one figure should be given full and blind applicability in all circumstances while the other should be inconsequential in circumstances which may frequently arise.
My second point is that in a case of doubt it is possible for us to go beyond the wording of the rule provided appropriate recognized guidance exists. In the case to which I refer we have the words of the preamble to the second report of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization presented March 14, 1975, the report which introduced these rules. The preamble reads:
(5) It is the view of your committee that the first hour of each sitting should normally be devoted to oral questions. It is recognized that some members believe that there is a constructive purpose in retaining proceedings pursuant to Standing Order 43 at the beginning of a sitting. There is a consensus, however, that most routine proceedings ought to be taken up at a set time, but after oral questions. There is a consensus that statements by ministers and responses thereto ought to be limited. Your committee is of the view that questions of privilege and points of order raised during the oral question period, unless Mr. Speaker considers it to be a most grave matter, ought to be taken up after the oral question period.
I draw attention particularly to the words "but after oral questions". That paragraph really sets the framework for subsequent interpretation, indicating that our whole procedure has been framed around the question period as the central feature of the parliamentary day, and it is important we should consider the matter in that light. It is obvious from the records of the committee and in the context of the paragraph I have read that the word "normally" was inserted to show that the committee intended the question period to last approximately an hour, as was fast becoming the practice at the time, but that it recognized that proposed motions under Standing Order 43 would sometimes take a few minutes. It was clearly not the intention that anything should arise which would have the effect of totally cancelling the question period.
The reason for inserting a preamble was made clear by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) who drafted the rules for the consideration of the committee. He said in the committee on March 4, 1975:
I think we understand what it is we want to do, but it may well be that other members and Mr. Speaker may not understand the intent. So we would want to draft a sort of preamble to the actual rules to make it quite clear what the intent is and the spirit in which the rules are to be interpreted.
There followed a brief exchange on March 10, 1975, which makes the spirit and intent clear:

The preamble was part of the report which was concurred in unanimously and without debate by the House, and is therefore a guide, as was intended, to the interpretation of the draft Standing Orders presented at the same time. That committee, of which I was a member at the time, and am now, operated in good faith, and I hope this continues to be the case.
Therefore I suggest that the starting time of 2.15 or 11.15 is as inviolable as the 3.00 p.m or 12 noon finishing time. It seems to me that if we are to give both boundaries their proper place, then if a motion under Standing Order 43 is put to the House, any debate, or any division, must be deferred until after question period and routine proceedings.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you find this a reasonable and acceptable interpretation of the rule which the procedure committee recommended to the House, and I hope if there is any discussion other members of that committee will confirm the spirit of our deliberations.
